candidateRows: The best explanation of all contingent things must be an automatically actual, noncontingent foundation rather than another contingent member of the totality.
This is the initial formulation of the contingency argument and directly supplies the inference from contingent reality to the proposed necessary or automatically actual foundation.
After introductions, Josh presents the argument as an inference to the best explanation and outlines why avoiding explanatory circularity leads beyond contingent things.
The argument can initially remain neutral among accounts of necessity while still inferring a noncontingent source through ordinary anti-circular explanatory reasoning.
The move answers a foundational challenge about what necessity means by defending a deliberately minimal first-stage conclusion that does not depend on one maximal modal account.
Scott's concern that the conclusion invokes an unclear necessary being and may conflate uncausedness with existence in every possible world.
Josh distinguishes the phrase automatically actual from stronger and potentially confusing notions of necessity, then restates the explanatory structure using ordinary objects as an analogy.
Explanatory intuitions that apply within material reality need not extend to spacetime or reality as a whole, and a foundational deity could instead exist as a brute fact.
This supplies the central skeptical alternative: deny that the demand for explanation scales to total reality and reject the inference from an ultimate foundation to modal necessity.
Josh's claim that the same anti-circular explanatory reasoning used for ordinary contingent objects can reveal a noncontingent source of contingent reality.
Scott grants much of the local explanatory reasoning but says his intuitions fail at the level of all material reality and questions what could make God exist in every possible world.
Necessity admits different strengths, so the argument may reject maximal epistemic certainty while retaining a weaker foundational status such as being unable to begin or cease.
The distinction blocks the objection that the argument requires an implausibly maximal necessity and identifies weaker common ground sufficient to continue investigating the foundation.
Scott's objection that conceivable worlds without God make it difficult to understand or accept the claim that God has to exist.
Josh separates logical or epistemic certainty, possible-world necessity, and factual necessity, using a dial metaphor to seek a defensible strength for the foundational conclusion.
Even if the universe began and is contingent, causal intuitions formed inside it may not govern its ultimate boundary, leaving the universe's brute existence plausible.
The move presents the principal brute-foundation alternative to the contingency inference and explains why ordinary causal expectations may lose authority at the beginning of spacetime.
The first-stage proposal that contingent reality should be explained by a necessary or automatically actual foundational layer.
Following a clarification that only stage one is under discussion, Scott grants for argument that the universe begins but doubts that familiar causal and explanatory intuitions apply there.
Careful inquiry into ultimate reality may legitimately extend the same inference-to-the-best-explanation practices used in science, favoring a robust foundation over brute contingency.
This directly defends the contested extension of explanatory reasoning to reality as a whole and supplies the abductive basis for preferring a foundational explanation to brute facts.
Scott's claim that human causal intuitions are grounded within the experienced universe and may not apply to its origin or ultimate structure.
Josh combines epistemic humility with confidence in limited reasoning about ultimate reality, then analogizes the contingency inference to scientific preference for available explanations.
Calling God's existence necessary does not itself explain why God exists, because the property of necessary existence appears available only conditional on God's already existing.
The challenge attacks the claimed explanatory advantage of a necessary foundation by arguing that necessity may merely redescribe an existing entity rather than explain its actuality.
Josh's proposal that an automatically actual foundation provides a better ultimate explanation of contingent reality than leaving reality unexplained.
Scott agrees that explanations are desirable but presses the regress-like question of what explains God, arguing that necessity cannot do the explanatory work assigned to it.
Necessary existence is explanatorily unsatisfying when it depends on the entity's existence, much as an effect cannot explain the condition invoked to account for that effect.
The analogy sharpens the conditionality objection and makes the skeptic's central complaint precise: necessity seems downstream from existence rather than an explanation of existence.
The contention that a foundation's necessary or automatically actual character can explain why it exists without any further external explanation.
Scott confirms that necessity is not a satisfying explanation and uses a damaged-car analogy to illustrate why reversing the apparent explanatory direction fails to improve understanding.
What specially calls for explanation is actuality that could have failed, whereas an automatically actual foundation avoids that demand and may have its necessity explained by supremacy.
This is the main direct answer to the explanatory objection, grounding differential explanatory demands in contingency and offering a further account connecting supreme nature to necessity.
Scott's claim that necessary existence cannot explain an entity's actuality because the entity must already exist before possessing necessity.
Josh asks what features call for explanation, argues that nonautomatic actuality creates a distinctive explanatory demand, and distinguishes explaining necessity from explaining contingent effects.
Explaining divine necessity through divine supremacy threatens circularity if necessary existence is itself one of the properties that makes the foundation supreme.

The move directly challenges Josh's proposed deeper explanation of necessity and tests whether the supreme-foundation account genuinely advances beyond unexplained necessity or merely circles back to it.
Josh's suggestion that a foundation's supreme nature can explain why it possesses a robust automatically actual or necessary nature.
Scott argues that necessity is ordinarily treated as greatness-making, so deriving necessity from supremacy appears circular, and he asks what fact makes divine existence necessary.
A necessary foundation may have no further explanation precisely because its existence is automatically actual, while a supreme nature could also explain its necessity.
This directly addresses whether the proposed necessary foundation must itself receive an explanation, a central stopping-point objection to the contingency argument.
Clifton's objection that deriving necessity from divine supremacy appears circular and leaves necessity itself unexplained.

Clifton challenges the explanatory direction between supremacy and necessity; Rasmussen allows the question but argues that the contingency argument can terminate at an automatically actual foundation.
Any contingent things have an explanation of their existence, and the explanation of all such things cannot itself be among the contingent things explained.
This supplies the operative explanatory principle and the inference from contingent reality to an explanation outside the contingent collection.
The request to clarify which causal or explanatory principle Rasmussen endorses for the contingency argument.
After several candidate principles are recalled, Rasmussen offers his preferred formulation and explains why its application to all contingent things points beyond them.
Brute contingency is explanatorily worse than brute necessity because an automatically actual foundation does not call for a deeper explanation in the way a contingent fact does.
The comparative plausibility of brute contingency and brute necessity is the core dialectical issue governing whether the contingency argument is persuasive.
Clifton's suggestion that accepting an unexplained necessary existence may simply amount to accepting another brute fact.
Rasmussen asks the participants to set God aside and imagine an ultimate automatically actual reality whose nonexistence is excluded by its own nature.
Contingency as failure to exist in every possible world need not imply dependence, so God could be independent yet exist in only some possible worlds as a brute modal fact.
This separates modal contingency from causal dependence and thereby challenges the inference from independence or ultimacy to necessary existence.
Rasmussen's claim that a merely contingent ultimate would still invite a deeper explanation in terms of something noncontingent.
Clifton warns that different senses of contingency may be conflated and proposes an independent but modally contingent God whose world-specific actuality is brute.
An objective and necessary logical landscape can belong to reality's foundational layer, with human reasoning tracking principles that remain true independently of human minds.
The move offers positive content for an automatically actual foundation and connects necessary logical reality to the first stage of the contingency argument.
Clifton's proposed distinction between causal dependence and modal necessity, and his request for the relevant account of possibility.
Rasmussen argues that logical truths correspond to mind-independent rules of reality and suggests these necessary rules are built into a supreme foundation.
Logic may govern statements and inference rather than constitute an ontological structure embedded in reality, since contradictions apply to linguistic claims rather than rocks or clocks.
This rejects the principal bridge from necessary logical truths to a necessary ontological foundation and thus undercuts Rasmussen's proposed stage-two support.
Rasmussen's claim that objective principles of logic form a necessary landscape within the fabric of reality's foundation.
Clifton accepts that consistent reasoning matters but doubts that logical laws exist as an extra ontological layer rather than as constraints on statements.
Necessary abstract truths can be explained through the contradiction entailed by their denial, but no analogous fact appears to make a concrete being such as God unable not to exist.
The objection directly contests the transition from acknowledged necessary abstract reality to the concrete necessary foundation required by the theistic conclusion.
Rasmussen's effort to unify necessary abstract propositions with a concrete necessary foundation containing the logical landscape.
Clifton contrasts the intelligible necessity of arithmetic with the absence of any contradiction or truth-maker establishing that a concrete God cannot fail to exist.

A supreme-foundation hypothesis predicts perfect principles of reasoning, while the proposition that nothing exists entails that something is true and therefore that something exists, yielding contradiction.
This responds to the abstract-concrete gap by combining an abductive prediction from supremacy with an argument that absolute nonbeing is contradictory.
Clifton's objection that no fact or contradiction appears capable of making a concrete being such as God necessarily existent.
Rasmussen says supremacy predicts rational structure and then argues through truth and existence that the statement asserting nothing exists defeats itself.

Conceivability of a godless world does not establish its genuine possibility because contradictions may emerge only through extended inference, and the contingency argument can independently indicate such a hidden contradiction.
This answers the modal-conceivability basis for denying necessary divine existence and assigns the contingency argument independent evidential force regarding necessity.
Clifton's claim that God's nonexistence is not self-contradictory and that nothing identifiable makes God unable not to exist.
Rasmussen argues that implicit contradictions may require multiple inferential steps, so apparent conceivability warrants agnosticism rather than a conclusion of metaphysical possibility.

Unknown empirical identities do not support hidden contradiction claims because statement meaning depends on intended content, as illustrated by a hindsight-free Twin Earth case involving consciousness.
The move challenges Rasmussen's appeal to contradictions beyond present comprehension by disputing the semantic mechanism that would turn undiscovered identities into contradictions.
Rasmussen's proposal that propositions can be contradictory despite our present inability to discover or comprehend the relevant inferential chain.
Clifton uses Twin Earth first with water and then without hindsight with consciousness, arguing that speakers using a mistaken identity claim would be wrong rather than self-contradictory.
An undecided mathematical conjecture illustrates that a contradiction can exist even when nobody presently recognizes it.
The example supports Rasmussen's account of unseen logical contradictions, which underlies his claim that necessity can outrun present conceivability or recognition.
Clifton's proposed consciousness counterexample to contradictions existing beyond what speakers can presently identify.
Clifton argues that future discoveries about consciousness would make earlier claims mistaken rather than self-contradictory; Rasmussen substitutes an unresolved mathematical conjecture.
Reality plausibly has an explanatory foundation whose nature may incorporate the strongest kind of necessity exemplified by logic.
This closing synthesis states the affirmative route from explanatory structure to a foundation and then toward a logically necessary character for that foundation.
After the moderator announces approaching closing remarks, Rasmussen summarizes areas of agreement and locates the remaining dispute in how much necessity reality's foundation possesses.
A brute foundation need not exist in every possible world, so moving from unexplained existence to necessary existence is unwarranted.
This is Clifton's principal closing objection to the motion: explanatory fundamentality or bruteness does not itself establish existence across all possible worlds.
Rasmussen's proposal that the explanatory foundation has a necessity comparable to the necessity associated with logical principles.
Clifton grants considerable common ground about a foundation but rejects the leap from its being brute or foundational to its existing necessarily in every possible world.
Calling the foundation brute means only that it has no further explanation, while a necessary nature distinguishes it from ordinary dependent things.
The distinction blocks an equivocation between being unexplained and being contingent, preserving Rasmussen's claim that necessity marks the foundation off from dependent reality.
Clifton's treatment of a brute God as merely happening to exist and therefore no longer existing of necessity.
Clifton suggests a brute God could be contingent; Rasmussen clarifies that bruteness concerns the absence of further explanation and is compatible with a necessary nature.
Necessary existence supplies no genuine explanation of why God exists, and comparable bruteness can be assigned to the universe instead.
The move attacks both explanatory necessity and the argument's discriminatory power, contending that its acceptable notion of a brute foundation favors neither God nor the universe.
Rasmussen's clarification that necessary nature differentiates an unexplained foundation from contingent dependent objects.
After Rasmussen distinguishes bruteness from contingency, Clifton argues that necessity explains nothing and that a universe can occupy the same brute-foundation role as God.
Treating the contingency argument as an inquiry into reality's structure gives reason to regard its foundation as more robust than an ordinary contingent object.
This reframes and defends the affirmative inference: if a merely contingent foundation would invite a better further explanation, the foundation has a more robust nature.
Clifton's contention that necessity does not explain God's existence and that the universe can serve equally well as a brute foundation.
Rasmussen temporarily brackets the word God, asks what the universe's foundational layer is like, and argues that ordinary contingency would leave room for further explanation.
The proposed foundation should remain classified as contingent because no concrete being has been shown capable of necessary existence.
The response refuses the key reclassification on which Rasmussen's structural progress depends, while limiting plausible necessity to abstract entities rather than concrete foundations.
Rasmussen's claim that openness to further explanation supports assigning the foundation a more robust, non-merely-contingent nature.
Clifton acknowledges Rasmussen's reframing but says he would place the foundation back among contingent things because concrete necessary existence remains unintelligible to him.
Clifton's resistance may arise from picturing concrete reality materially, whereas God can be conceived as a nonmaterial supreme conceptual reality with causal power.
The diagnosis attempts to dissolve the intuitive barrier to concrete necessity by separating the proposed foundation from material objects that both speakers accept are contingent.
Clifton's assertion that the foundation must be contingent because he cannot see how any concrete being could exist necessarily.

Following Clifton's restriction of necessity largely to abstract things, Rasmussen suggests that a nonmaterial, mind-like, conceptually structured concrete reality may support different modal intuitions.
The contingency argument can rationally move people toward a necessary being without compelling every rational person to accept its conclusion.
This is Rasmussen's explicit final answer to the debate question, defining the relevant standard of persuasiveness and claiming both personal and reported persuasive effects.
Prompted by the moderator's observation that the stated question remained unanswered, Rasmussen says the argument need not force assent to count as genuinely persuasive.
The argument remains unpersuasive because proposition-like abstract entities are themselves doubtful, though granting them would provide a basis for further inquiry.
This closing response identifies Clifton's remaining obstacle to persuasion while conceding the conditional significance of the premise for a later argument about the foundation's personhood.
Rasmussen's closing claim that the contingency argument can move rational people toward belief in a necessary being without forcing assent.
Clifton closes by maintaining skepticism about treating propositions as existing abstract things, while acknowledging that accepting them would make a second-stage discussion worthwhile.
